summary:
Use the rotated-search idea (one half around mid is sorted, check whether the target fits its range). Repeats
add one ambiguous case: when `a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi]` you can't tell which half is sorted, so shrink both ends
by one. Average O(log n), worst O(n), which is unavoidable here.

question.md:
Ids were sorted non-decreasingly (repeats allowed), then rotated. Return true if `target` is on the shelf.

- **Repeats can hide the structure:** `[1, 0, 1, 1, 1]` and `[1, 1, 1, 0, 1]` look identical at lo, mid and hi.
- **Worst case O(n) is unavoidable:** an all-equal shelf with one different id could hide it anywhere.
- **Only true/false** is needed, which makes discarding duplicate positions harmless.

think.md:
Take `[6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 1, 3, 6, 6]` and target 3. At the start, a[lo], a[mid] and a[hi] are all 6. Here the drop is in the right
half, but the shelf `[6, 1, 3, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6]` shows exactly the same three values with the drop on the left.
`a[lo] ≤ a[mid]` (6 ≤ 6) can't distinguish the two.

think.caption: Equal values at lo, mid and hi: no way to tell where the drop is.

think.md:
In that situation, neither end can be the target (they equal a[mid], which we already checked), so **drop both
ends** and look again. When the three values aren't all equal, `a[lo] ≤ a[mid]` once again reliably means the
left half is sorted, and the distinct-values logic applies.

approaches.title: Linear search
build: Return true if any id equals the target.

lines.text: Every position is compared with the target.

limits.md: Always linear, even on shelves with few repeats where O(log n) is possible.

approaches.title: Rotated search with duplicate shrinking

idea.md: Same as the distinct case, but first check `a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi]`: if so, `lo += 1`, `hi −= 1` and continue.

build: All three equal → shrink both ends.
Else decide the sorted half with `a[lo] ≤ a[mid]` and test the target's range.

lines.text: Ambiguous: the sorted half can't be identified. The ends equal a[mid], which isn't the target, so they can't be the target either; drop both.
Now `a[lo] ≤ a[mid]` reliably means the left half is sorted (the all-equal case is gone). Go left only if the target is in its range.
Otherwise the right half is sorted; same test.

complexity.md: **Time O(log n)** typically, **O(n)** when the shrink case repeats (many equal ids). **Space O(1).**

steps.text: lo=0, hi=8, mid=4: a[lo] = a[mid] = a[hi] = 6; neither half can be proven sorted. Neither end is the target, so drop both: lo=1, hi=7.
lo=1, hi=7, mid=4: a[lo] = a[mid] = a[hi] = 6; neither half can be proven sorted. Neither end is the target, so drop both: lo=2, hi=6.
lo=2, hi=6, mid=4: left half sorted (6…6); target outside → right.
lo=5, hi=6, mid=5: left half sorted (1…1); target outside → right.

walk.title: Sorted-half search, plus one rule: if a[lo], a[mid] and a[hi] are all equal, shrink both ends by one.

takeaways.md:
- Duplicates add one case to rotated search: `a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi]` → shrink both ends.
- Expect a linear worst case whenever equal values can mask the structure.
